subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a new member I
had not intended to take part in this debate, but inasmuch as several statements have been made that are calculated to mislead the public, especially in connection with Ontario affairs'
I deem it my duty to say a few words in connection with the same.
But before going on to discuss Canadian affairs I ask that I be permitted to say a few words in connection with the trouble threatening the Old Country at the present time. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that I express the views

of every member on both sides of this House when I say that I hope the clouds now hovering over Great Britain will soon be dispelled, and that a better understanding between the parties to this great conflict will soon be arrived at. In this regard I notice evidences of an inclination on the part of some people in Canada to attribute ulterior motives to both sides. There are a great many persons in Canada who have blood relations and dear friends in the old land who feel impelled to express their views on the question. I think upon reflection, however, we will all agree that heated argument upon this side of the Atlantic, especially at the present stage of affairs, will do very little good. I am sure it is the desire of everyone to abstain from any action which might be productive of harm and to do nothing which would delay the early conclusion of a settlement honourable to both sides. I have great faith in the ability of the British people to overcome difficulties no matter how grave they may be, and I sincerely hope that no words will be expressed on this side of the ocean other than words of encouragement and helpfulness in the expectation that both sides of the controversy may soon get together and settle the dispute in a way that will be mutually fair and honourable.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Maloney) yesterday delivered what I may call a nice little speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, it was a nice little political speech, and I desire to congratulate the hon. member upon it. It was too bad, however, that the hon. gentleman had to bring in the labour trouble in Nova Scotia in order to make political capital. In bis effort to do that the hon. gentleman misinterpreted the whole situation as it existed there. I agree entirely with the hon. gentleman that there was no need to order troops into Nova Scotia on the occasion referred to. But seeing that troops were ordered there, the hon. gentleman should have truthfully stated how that came about. I think the hon. gentleman stated yesterday that this government had ordered the troops to be sent to Nova Scotia, and had instructed them to shoot. The hon. gentleman followed this up by stating that the soldiers did shoot and that bloodshed had followed. My information is that there was no shooting on the occasion in question and consequently no bloodshed. The Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior both undertook to explain to the hon. gentleman who was responsible for the ordering out of the troops. May I now supplement what they said. The law specifically places the

The Budget-Mr. Heenan
responsibility of ordering out troops on the shoulders of the attorney general of each province. The act which deals with the matter is the Militia Act which was amended in 1924. Section 81 of that act reads as follows:
In any case where a riot or disturbance occurs, or is anticipated as likely to occur, the attorney general or the acting attorney general of the province in which is situated the place where such riot or disturbance occurs or is anticipated as likely to occur on his own motion or upon receiving notification from a judge of a superior or county or district court, having jurisdiction in such place, that the services of the active militia are required in aid of the civil power may by requisition in writing addressed to the district officer commanding the military district in which such place is situated, require the active militia or such portion thereof as the district officer commanding considers necessary, to be called out on active service in aid *of the civil power.
The next section, section 82, points out that if the district officer commanding a military [DOT]district is not present, or is unable to act from sickness or any other cause, the officer for the time being commanding shall call out the active militia. There is no discretion in the matter, the officer commanding is obligated to call out the militia when he receives a requisition from the attorney general.

speechtext:
Pardon me; I did not
mean that to be a smart answer to the hon. member (Mr. Quinn); I was answering the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Maloney), who spoke yesterday about what happened a year ago in Nova Scotia. During the Winnipeg strike I was there; our men kept out of the strike. Therefore, I know something about it, and I know there was no more need for troops in the Winnipeg strike in 1919 than there was for troops in Nova Scotia last year. I am simply trying to get the facts before the people. All that was necessary in the Winnipeg trouble was that the Minister of Labour, who was on the job, should have used a little horse sense, and there would have been no blood shed. But instead of that, they chose to have the troops sent in. It was premeditated, it does not make very much difference, because I think if hon. members on the other side would allow the files to be brought down they would find it was all premeditated, that when the boys were being discharged or demobilized on their landing, special men who would do their bidding, were picked out to be sent to Winnipeg, and they were very careful that those who, they thought, would not do their bidding were not sent. I say the government is entirely responsible for that.
I desire to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his financial statement, and I do this very sincerely, because I consider that $22,000,000 of a surplus is something that any government might be proud of. I notice that hon. members in their speeches find different excuses why this government should not receive credit for having a surplus. I have often thought it is too bad that public men, men who aspire to be statesmen, should become so partisan in their views that they cannot even give credit where credit is due.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the other day in an effort to throw cold water on the surplus, actually

The Budget-Mr. Heenan
compared the financial affairs of the Dominion with that of Ontario. He said that while the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was satisfactory at least to some extent, they could not give any credit to the government; that the credit was all due to Providence for giving a bountiful crop. On the other hand and almost in the next breath he lauded the financial condition of Ontario, and while admitting that that province had also a great crop and that Providence had been kind to Ontario, he gave the credit to the financial experts of the Conservative government of Ontario. This is what the hon. member said when he was speaking of economy:
If there is one thing which the people of this country demand at the present time, it is that the expenditure of the national government be cut down. I know of no cry throughout the province of Ontario more persistent than that government economy be exercised to the very last degree. We hear that cry in our provincial legislature, and we are pleased to note that the government of Ontario has put the finances of the province on such a footing that within a reasonable time that province will regain its former financial stability.
I was a member of the Ontario legislature for six years, resigning my seat to run in the last election. My position has not yet been filled; the government of to-day apparently consider that the north country is just as well off without a representative as with one. I would at least have thought they would try to get a Conservative to represent that district because even a Conservative is a little better than no representative. Having an interest in the financial condition of that province I secured a copy of the public accounts and this is what I find. At the end of 1922, which was the last full year of the Drury regime, the total debt of the province amounted to $240,506,176. At the end of 1925, after three years' administration of the economical Conservative government, the total debt amounted to $324,922,473, or an increase of $84,416,297.

Peter Smiths only they have not been caught The hon. member for South Wellington says that the cry for economy prevails all through the province of Ontario. Let us see how this economical Conservative government answered that cry for economy. In 1922 the Drury government spent $37,000,000; in 1925, in answer to this cry for economy, the Ferguson government spent $51,000,000. I ask again, if that is the way in which the hon. member for South Wellington would like this government to economize, that is by continuing to increase expenditure notwithstanding the fact that the public debt is increasing. The Ferguson government collected $6,000,000 more from the people last year than they did in 1924 and $12,500,000 more than they did in 1923 and yet they show a deficit of $5,000,000. Is that the way in which the hon. member for South Wellington would like this government to carry on the finances of this country? As a comparison with the Drury regime because I notice the provincial treasurer all through his speech made a comparison with the last horrible year, as the Conservatives call it, of the Drury regime, I should like to point out that if last year the Tory government of Ontario had received only the same amount of money as the Drury government did in 1923 and spent the same amount as they did in 1925, they would have shown a deficit of $17,500,000 last year instead of $5,000,000.

discussing provincial and not federal politics, what was the actual deficit in the last year of the so-called Drury regime?

I am glad my hon. friend asked me that question because I might have forgotten it. As regards discussing provincial politics I am answering one of my hon. friend's friends who tried to tell this country that the finances of Ontario are in good shape and that this government should copy that province. Hon. members will recall that the
The Budget-Mr. Heenan

provincial election took place in June, 1923, and the government changed hands in July. The Drury government spent a good deal of money that year, but hon. members will have to admit that the Tory government not only kept the books, but fixed them so that they made it the most horrible year it was possible to make it. They paid every cent they could find to pay and they urged everybody to put in their bills, saying: The going is good; come on in. On the other hand it was generally known that they encouraged people who owed money to the government to withhold their payments until the end of the fiscal year when the books were closed. It was therefore by cooking it in this way that the Conservative government of Ontario was able to show that the Drury government had practically a deficit of $15,000,000.

After manipulating the finances of the province in this way the Conservative government of the province then compared their record with that of the Drury government, but I would again point out that if they had received only the same amount in 1925 as the Drury government received in 1923 and spent the same amount as they did, they would have a deficit of $17,500,000 in the past year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not as bad as nineteen and a half million.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But the whole story is not told merely by showing the deficit. The Conservative government of the province has persistently asserted that what it was able to accomplish it accomplished without creating new taxes. It has successfully fooled the people. The press comes out with headlines like these:
No new taxes. Old deficit cut'. Surplus of two
pillion dollars.
The press can publish these headlines for the simple reason that the government of the province gives out intimations to this effect long before the legislature gets the public accounts. Evidently there is method in their madness, for they have misled the press.
The Ferguson government did double the dues on timber last year and that is a new tax, and they put on a new tax on gasoline and beer from which they received $1,174,000. They might have got more out of the beer had it been good beer, but the fact is that the people of Ontario have been just as greatly disappointed in their 4.4 as they have been in the Ferguson government. The Fer-

guson government also benefited by an increase in motor permits to the extent of $850,000, and in succession duties they received an additional $1,600,000. A number of rich people having died, the government col-' lected the taxes from their estates; and I hardly think that the hon. member for South Wellington had that in his mind when he said that Providence had been good to the Ferguson government. The Minister of Finance is not in his place, and so I will address this appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King): Do not let the government accept the views of financial experts from Ontario as a basis for them to go upon.
I do not think that we ought to dispose of the question of Ontario's finances without considering the way in which some of the money has been spent. I suppose it is general knowledge that in Ontario we have what is known as the northern development fund. It is usually supplemented to the extent of $5,000,000. The legislature votes the money in a lump sum, placing it in charge of the Minister of Lands and Forests, so that the government or the minister has a blank cheque for $5,000,000, which is supposed to be used for the development of fifteen districts in northern Ontario in respect of roads, bridges and so forth. These districts are each supposed to get a square deal in this matter. But do they? I want to tell the House that during the past three years this development fund has been used mainly for the purpose of corrupting the electorate of northern Ontario, and I make that statement after giving the matter due consideration. I say it knowing the responsibility of a public man in making a statement of the kind. The fund has been used mainly for the purpose of corrupting the electorate of northern Ontario and when such corruption has failed it has been used in order to intimidate, to discriminate against, and even to persecute settlers in the. north country.

In order to prove my
case, let me say that one of the reasons I resigned my seat in the provincial legislature .was in order to run in the federal election last year and protest against these practices that were going on, to protest against using public money to bring settlers into new Ontario from the Old Country, and sending them out into New Ontario when they got here and telling them to hew a farm out of the bush, and then have the hired thugs of the provincial government go amongst them and tell them that they would not get a square deal until they voted a Conservative in for that particular riding. That was one of the issues in the district that I had the honour to represent. Notwithstanding the fact that the machine went up there, and that these hired thugs went all over the district, the people of that provincial riding gave me a majority of nearly eight hundred. This confirms the statement I am making on the floor of this House. Now, there are none
l Mr. Heenan.]
so blind as those who will not see. It was well known to every Conservative in that part of the province that an issue would be made of these doings when the proper time came. As a matter of fact when I ran in the election I did so as a protest against such methods, and I hope opposition members in this House from the province of Ontario will take notice of the verdict w'hich the people rendered on the occasion referred to, and that all such practices will be strictly tabooed by them in the future. When I accepted the nomination for the riding we knew that one of the gang, or one of the advisers of the provincial government, intended to secure the nomination for the Conservative party. It was in order to keep that man out of public life-a man who would so far forget himself as to lend himself to the designs of a gang that would advise any government, whether Liberal or Conservative, to persecute the settlers in the northern country-that I offered myself as a candidate, and I succeeded in defeating him. There is one more member of the gang now before the public for the next provincial election, but I am quite content to leave him in the hands of the people of the district.
A comparison has been made between the way in which the finances of Ontario are administered by the provincial government and the method adopted by the federal administration. The hon. member for South Wellington, for example, made such a comparison. I ask that hon. gentleman to state whether he would follow the financial methods of the present Ontario government if he were on the federal benches, or whether he would use the public money in the way in which I have stated it has been used by the Ontario government? I think I have a right to ask that question, and that it is a perfectly fair one in view of the statements which some hon. gentlemen opposite have made.
The hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), during his speech on the evening of Friday last, gave utterance to the following statement:
New Ontario has been economically annexed to the United States. Why do I say that? Because New Ontario has been a happy hunting ground for American millionaires for years past. Mr. Drury, the former Premier of Ontario, gave to Mr. Backus, a Milwaukee millionaire, an enormous timber area, an empire in itself.
I had been under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservatives advocated a policy of establishing industries to manufacture raw materials of Canada in this country. I had thought that hon. gentlemen

The Budget-Mr. Heenan
329.1
opposite advocated the adoption of a tariff as would compel Americans to establish industries in this country, rather than permit the exportation of Canadian raw material to the country to the south to be manufactured and to give employment to American work-ment there. It is very difficult to follow the varying arguments of successive Conservative speakers. On the one hand they say "Let us have such a tariff that American capitalists will be forced to establish factories in Canada and give employment to Canadian workmen." On the other hand, when American millionaires are induced to locate in Canada, they set up the cry that we are being annexed to the United States. Really it is very difficult to follow such arguments or to find any harmony between them. However, I am getting used to inconsistencies of this kind on the part of Conservatives. It is true that the Drury government did sell a timber limit to Mr. Backus in 1921. One would think that the Conservatives-of course I have special reference to those in Ontario-were loath to do business with Mr. Backus either through fear or some other cause. But what are the facts? We find that they did do business with Mr. Backus only they went about it in a different way from that adopted by the Drury government. The latter government disposed of a timber limit openly, to Mr. Backus; the whole transaction was open and aboveboard. But how did the present Conservative government act in their dealings with Mr. Backus? At the last session of the legislature before the last federal election the Minister of Lands and Forests announced, amid a loud beating of drums, that no doubt the people of Ontario would be glad to know that the government had cancelled some water powers granted to Mr. Backus by Mr. Drury. The announcement was followed by such a rattling of desks on the part of the Conservatives that that furniture was in imminent danger of destruction. But strange to say, after the election was over, the same minister returned the same water powers to Mr. Backus. The people of the district were not aware that such a thing had been done. Even the mayor of Fort Frances, although the town was particularly interested in the agreement with Mr. Backus, was not aware of it. Worse than all, the Premier of the province made the humiliating confession that he did not even know that negotiations had been going on for the return of these water powers and was entirely in the dark as to the transaction. This was about two weeks before the then Minister of Lands and Forests resigned.
Now, I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, from Ontario, this question:	When they do
business with Mr. Backus, or any other millionaire, is it better to act in an open and straightforward fashion or to work in a stealthy, secret manner? If my hon. friends will refer to the Toronto Telegram of March 15, they will see where the Premier of On-, tario made the humiliating confession, that he did not know that the transaction referred to had taken place. I am not discussing whether it was advisable to enter into the arrangement or not. Personally I think that a man who spends thirty, or forty or fifty-million dollars in establishing paper mills in Ken or i, as Mr. Backus did, who gives employment to about two thousand men, and who pays about $40,000 in taxes for a period of ten years, ought to be encouraged. But when we do business with him we should do. it openly so that the public shall have full and complete knowledge of what is going on. No public matter should be handled according to the backdoor methods practised by the Conservative party in the. province of Ontario, It is not generally known that the Hearst government, in which Mr. Ferguson was Minister of Lands and Forests, sold Mr. Backus, a timber limit in 1914.

speechtext:
I commenced by complimenting the Minister of Finance on his budget, and I proceeded to answer the hon. member for South Wellington when he advised the Minister of Finance to copy the financial policy of the province of Ontario*
The Budget-Mr. Heenan

He made certain statements, and I think it is only fair that they should be answered. I do not think that one party should get what they wish on Hansard and that the other party should be ruled out of order and prevented from answering. The 'hon. member for Toronto Northwest made a speech on Friday night in which he made certain charges; another hon. member asked some questions in connection with his remarks, and I am trying to .answer those questions. Surely, if a member is permitted to ask a question I should be allowed to answer it, and I can assure hon. members that before I get through I will connect this matter with Dominion affairs. I am just wondering whether my appeal to the House will be of any value, because an hon. member for one of the Ontario constituencies has stated that I have been making statements and charges that are without foundation. I have already told him that I have affidavits and documents to substantiate every charge I have made. It is the old saying, there are none so blind as those who will see. It is not generally known that the Ontario government sold Mr. Backus 2,000 square miles in 1914, and made a contract which permitted him to build a mill or not to build it just as he wished, and according to the agreement the mill was to be built on this 2,000 square miles or in the vicinity of it. They led the people .of Kenora to believe that the industry was to be established in that town. That is the whole trouble in connection with the matter the hon. member for Toronto Northwest spoke about on Friday night. An agreement was made, and I was present at all the proceedings. We made an agreement by which the water powers of the province of Ontario were disposed of, and the powers in the vicinity of Kenora were safeguarded. Not a pound of pulpwood was to be exported to the American side, and no power can be exported; everything is to be manufactured in Ontario. I want my friends on the other side of the House to advise the Ontario government to please copy, because they have not been doing it.
I feel sure that every hon. member will be glad to see the progress that our railroads are making in this country. I refer to Dominion, not to provincial roads. When we find that there is an increase of practically nine and a half million dollars in last year's revenue, with a decrease in working expenses of five and a half million dollars, making a betterment of approximately fifteen million dollars, I think there is room for gratification in connection with our railroad operation, indicating as it does wise management and loyal co-operation on the part of the workmen. It shows efficiency in every degree. As
{Mr. Heenan..]
an indication of the efficiency with which our railways have been operated, the employees moved nine and a half million dollars more of revenue bearing freight with a less consumption of coal to the extent of one and three-quarter million dollars, which again shows great efficiency in the operation of our road.
In looking over the yearly reports, Mr. Speaker, I was glad to see that the presidents of both roads give great credit to the employees. I observe that Sir Henry Thornton, in one paragraph of his report, stated that they are now considering the consolidation of the different pensions schemes throughout the system. There are different pensions schemes on the different branches of the Canadian National Railways, and I am satisfied that when these are consolidated we will have a pension system second to none in existence. I think hon. members will agree with me that the workmen on the Canadian National Railways who are showing such loyalty are entitled to this pension. I do not intend to go through the report, because I feel satisfied that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will deal with it in detail. I want to point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway report, while not presented with so much detail, shows they made $853,000 last year over and above the preceding year, but they cut down $2,074,000 in expenses, or, in other words, they laid off a great many of their employees altogether. They put a good many of them on short time, and in other ways helped to keep down the expense, so that they were able to show a surplus of $2,927,000 over the preceding year. That shows again loyalty and efficiency on the part of the men engaged in the transportation of the commerce of this country. The men who are employed on the railroad and are so loyal to their employers should not be subjected to this unwarranted, misleading propaganda that is being distributed through the country. I have before me Railway Bulletin No. 5, of the Railway Users Association of Canada. They endeavour to show that the government of this country had more to do with the increase in freight rates than any other factor. But I am wondering when the government really had anything to do with the increase. The bulletin goes on to state that there are 20,000 more people employed on the Canadian National Railways than there ought to be, it does not mention the fact that 3,000 fewer men were employed on that railroad last year than the year before. In connection with the Canadian Pacific pension plan, there is one regrettable feature which I feel it is my duty to mention at this time, namely, that the regulations pertaining to it provide that if an employee breaks his continuity of service he becomes deprived of his pension. We have an example at the present time of how this rule is applied. No doubt hon. members will remember that in 1908 the machinists and carmen went on strike. This strike was legal in every respect; the laws of the country and the laws pertaining to the constitution of those engaged in the strike were observed. And now eighteen years afterwards we find that many of these men, having contributed to the upbuilding and prosperity of the company, are reaching the age of sixty-five years and are being taken from their work and deprived of their pensions.
I am not going to argue at this time that the public is contributing to this fund through freight, passenger and other rates, or that the government should take a hand in the matter. I feel that all that is necessary at present is to draw the attention of the head officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway to this matter in the hope that they will give it their due consideration. I think I know the company well enough to believe that when we appeal to a big-hearted man like Mr. E. W. Beatty and his associate officials, they will rise to the occasion and be too big to hold spite at the end of eighteen years and discriminate against their old employees. I sincerely hope before we meet next session this grievance will be eliminated.

I had not thought I was doing so, because, as I said before, I was answering questions that had been raised by members of the opposition. I felt it was my duty to do this and any statements that I have made I am prepared to prove.

I have observed from time to time that members on the other side of the House have deplored the fact that the tariff on automobiles has been cut; not one of them that I have heard has yet stated that the duty ought not to be cut.
The amendment to the motion would, I think, make a man vote for the budget rather than against it because it is a compliment to the government. Any member who votes for the amendment surely votes confidence in the board that has been constituted. That is the way in which I view the amendment so that the government may take what consolation they like out of that. If I were in the Ontario legislature I would be permitted to say that the amendment was a "4.4" amendment; there was no body to it, and therefore if anything were necessary to enable me to reach a decision as to how to vote, it would be the amendment.
It is very difficult for a man who is listening to arguments in an endeavour to arrive at a conclusion, to determine how best to vote when he finds that on the resolution of last year in favour of cutting the tariff on automobiles, six Conservatives voted to reduce the tariff and some of them were re-elected as protectionists. Again, I am informed that the hon. member who represented Oshawa on the Liberal side last year put up a very hard fight in this House against any cut in the tariff on-automobiles, and yet he was defeated by his own people in the last election. I think, Mr. Speaker, that in describing the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Heenan) in the way you did, you will probably meet with the approval of the House. Certainly it was an address that might properly be termed rambling, for his remarks had reference to matters that do not appertain to this House in the slightest degree. This hon. gentleman who has just spoken was a supporter of the Drury government and if there was any one man in Ontario who contributed to the defeat of that government, it was the hon. member himself. He tells ua that he was mixed up with the Backus deal, that he was in on that transaction. That is generally understood in our province; it is known that he was very much in on that transaction. And that was one of the reasons why the Drury government went down to defeat. This hon. gentleman supported a government one of whose ministers, the provincial treasurer, ran the province into the hole and himself into gaol. This is the kind of man that comes here and in this parliament defends the Drury government. The proper place for him to have made his defence was in the legislature which he left. Why did he leave that legislature? Why was he not man enough to make his charges there instead of coming here for the express purpose of discussing the subject? He talks about blanket money being voted. I can tell the hon. member that he will have an opportunity to make all the protests he wants against blanket propositions when the estimates are before this House for consideration. If he wants to put as much ginger into opposition against blanket votes as he shows to-day he will have his opportunity here; he does not have to go to Ontario to do it. The hon. member tells us that he stood up in meetings with Mr. Drury, *but this deal was called the Raney-Backus deal. Mr. Drury was not mixed up in it for he would not go in with the bunch of people who were in on it. The hon. member tells us that he was well in on the deal, and as I say that was pretty well understood. He also tells us that he does not know very much about the automobile business, having to take his information from older members. Well,

here is a labour man coming into the House and in face of a deputation of thousands of people, all workers who are seeking their rights, he has not one solitary word to say in their behalf. That is the kind of labour man who represents or pretends to represent labour in this House.
The hon. member has referred, as other hon. gentlemen have frequently referred in the course of this debate, to Providence having helped the government. For this budget we have evidently two benefactors to thank- one the government, and the other Providence. A charming gentleman, an old member of the House, said the other day that he thanked Providence for being on the side of the government. Well, I am willing to give Providence all the credit, and I go further and thank Providence that things are not worse. This is not the first time that we have heard of this government invoking Providence. If I remember rightly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in a speech in one of the constituencies near Toronto, probably North Bay, called upon Providence to help him out of a difficult situation. According to a. newspaper report:
Mr. King pressed the point that under the constitution the Senate could not be reformed except from the outside. "I cannot ask the Governor General to let me appoint senators," he said jocularly; "I can only pray lervently to Providence to take away some of the old ones."
So that Providence has been invoked to>
remove senators from this sphere in order to-allow Liberals to be appointed in their stead.. Just imagine invoking Providence to have Mr. Duncan Marshall made a senator! It only remains for the government to supplicate Heaven to remove another senator to make room for "the Honourable" W. T. R. Preston. The newspaper report of this particular speech of the Prime Minister tells us that he made the remark "jocularly". I have heard of ministers making remarks ironically, but I am at a loss to see any occasion for jocularity in a prime minister's attitude to Providence. I have seen the right hon. gentleman here for quite a number of years, and I must say that I have never seen him in a jocular mood while on his feet. It may be that he is more jocular when'he gets down on his knees.
The last time I had the honour to address this House at any length I was invited by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) to read from the farmers' platform what they had to say therein on the plunder on boots and shoes. I did not then have the time to go into the question, and besides I made it clear that there were other members quite as well qualified as I was to deal with the subject, indeed, better qualified inasmuch as they had

a greater knowledge of the business. I have not heard anyone opposite say one word in defence of this industry from the standpoint of the tariff. Well, there will be one protectionist in the cabinet, but he may be a furniture protectionist. The article in the farmers' platform which I desire to read is headed, "Plunder on Boots and Shoes." The hon. member for Rosetown wanted me to put before the House what the farmers had to say in this regard; he wanted me to show what was their attitude to the boot and shoe tariff. The article is a follows:
Let us consider somewhat more specifically just what the protective tariff costs the people of Canada and how it affects wages. The census bureau gives the following daia on the Canadian boot and shoe industry for the census year 1910:
Value of home-made product	$33,967,248
Number of employees	 17,227
Salaries and wages paid	 $7,698,333
During the year ending March 31, 1911, Canada imported $2,045,835 worth of boots and shoes, the duty upon which was $585,996.71.
In that year the Dominion imported six times the value of boots and shoes from the United States that it did from Britain, and paid duty thereon amounting to $522,809.70, equal to 30 per cent.
The value of the domestic product for that year is given as $33,967,248, of which $60,935 was exported.
Now if our contention is sound that the manufacturers add the full amount of their protection to the selling price of the commodity when disposed of in the home market, the people of Canada paid for that year by way of taxes the following sums:
Customs duties	$	585.996 71
To the manufacturers	 10,177,893 90

Wages and salaries paid	 7.698,333 00

That is to say the Canadian people paid by way of taxes directly and indirectly more than $3,000,000 in excess of the total wages and salaries received by employees in the boot and shoe industry during the same period.
If we were to consider the interest of the country and of the wage-earning classes alone it would have paid the people to have scrapped every boot and shoe
factory in the land, handed over the workers their full wages and to have paid a direct subsidy to the government of more than $3,000,000, and the nation would have gained enormously thereby, especially if the artisan had been put at some truly productive work.
That in short, is an example of the principle laid down in this book. I did not hear any great applause when I read that article; many times before when this has been read my hon. friends to the left have applauded loudly. I would not expect to get so much applause from hon. friends opposite in that little Saskatchewan corner, but they believe in the very same principle.

There is one thing they omitted to answer in that article. In the last clause, as you will notice, they say, "and the nation would have gained enormous/ly, especially if the artisan had been put at some truly productive work." Would my hon. friend who just interrupted tell me what productive work he would give these seventeen thousand artisans, after having closed these factories? What will become of them if that policy is carried out? They will go, as thousands of others have gone, to the United States; they will leave this country if they cannot get work.
As I said before, that illustrates the principle, and now I will read for the benefit of the House how that principle was demonstrated in connection with the boot and shoe proposition:
As already explained, under a system of protection the consumer is compelled to pay a tax upon all imported goods that come under the tariff schedule. Upon all goods of domestic origin, produced under a protective system, the consumer must likewise pay a tax-although in this case the revenue finds its way to the bank account of private individuals alone.
I might expect my hon. friends to say that that is all right, but I want to illustrate this principle by taking another line of commodities, because it will be noticed that this booklet says, "any commodity that comes under the tariff schedule." I will give as an example the class of goods produced by the farmers, and we will see how it works out. It is said that one way of proving or disproving a case is to prove it absurd, and I will leave it to the House to judge whether or not this proves

to be an absurdity. The total value of agricultural products in Canada according to the year book of 1924, which is the. latest one from which I could get complete 5 p.m. figures, amounted to $1,708,000,000.
The total export of farm products for that year was valued at $503,391,402, so after deducting the exports from the total production you get the home consumption Consequently the amount consumed within Canada totalled about $1,205,000,000. Following tihe same method of calculation, during the year we imported from the United States a total of $65,546,476; from the United Kingdom $64,324,300, and from other countries as well, making a total importation of $149,201,231 of agricultural products similar to those raised in Canada. On a basis of 600.000 farmers in Canada this would mean that each farmer got $400 of extra money. He still had the money from the goods he had exported; he had the money from the produce sold in Canada, but in addition to that he had another $400. I do not think it does, but whether it does or does not has no relation at all to the argument I am making-not one particle. If the hon. gentleman wants to take out the $19,000,000, he is perfectly free to do so, and I will figure out for him how it works out.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted, according to this calculation- and it is based upon the principle laid dowr. in this platform-each farmer in this country not only got the money for the products he-exported and for the products he sold in this country, but in addition he filched out of the pockets of the people by way of plunder- that is the word they use-another $240,000,000 that did not belong to him, and which came out of the poor consumer of this country. That is the kind of argument these gentlemen put up. And this book, Mr. Speaker, is well edited. It is called the Farmers' Platform. It was drafted by the Canadian Council of Agriculture, and has been adopted by the United Farmers of Alberta, the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association and the United Farmers of Ontario. I do not hear anybody getting up and cheering about the argument this book puts forward.
Now let us take another example. Let us take apples, for instance, just to show in a small way how it works out. In 1924 we imported 195,000 barrels of apples, and the duty collected was $176,000. Our total average crop-I have not seen this year's returns, but I have looked over the figures for a number of years-runs to about five or six million barrels, but taking the lower figure,
5,000,000 barrels, we exported last year 1,600,000 barrels, which would leave for home consumption 3,400,000 barrels. Now the same contention is there. According to this book, on every barrel of these apples sold for home consumption the producer put 90 cents more in his pocket. I wish to heaven, Mr. Speaker, that these gentlemen could convince our farmers in Ontario that they had received that money; I wish they could bring it to pass. But don't you see, Mr. Speaker, the thing is absurd? But it is not a bit nor a whit more absurd than the argument on the boot and shoe proposition that is made all over the country, and which we hear in this House particularly from the new members for Saskatchewan. The gentlemen to my left

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin (Lincoln)
do not give us that argument any more; they know better now; they have learned their lesson.
I want to refer now to some of the remarks of the Finance minister, and first of all to his statement about the increased business of the country. The minister laid some stress upon the fact that the balance of trade was very much in our favour. First of all, let me say that I do not disagree with that statement, but I do submit this, that if it is a good thing generally to have a balance of trade in our favour, then it is a good thing to have a favourable balance of trade with our largest customer. That is a sound proposition. What do we find in respect to our trade with the United States? Our exports last year increased $57,000,000, and our imports increased $100,000,000; in other words, in one year the balance of trade against us increased by $43,000,000. In 1926, to the end of March, they sold us $609,000,000 worth of goods, and we exported to them $474,000,000 worth. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if it is a good thing, if it is logical and right, to have the balance of trade in your favour, then you had better have it in your favour as regards the people who are doing everything they can to hammer your heads off.
Let us take a few of our exports, in which we had an increase of $57,000,000, and see what they consisted of. I shall run over them briefly as I do not wish to take up very much

We have a big plant at Niagara Falls, and we ship them the raw fertilizer and buy back the finished product. This government within the last year or so has put out of business ten fertilizer plants in this country. This one plant remains in business at Niagara Falls, using an immense quantity of power, and the fertilizer in the shape of ammonium sulphate and cyanamide is going over to the United States to be further manufactured.
Our exports of grain products increased by $3,400,000, and of grain, $4,000,000. Our exports of wheat increased, in bushels, from
5,400,000	to 9,200,000. Our exports of oats decreased by 4,000,000 bushels. Why? They did not take our oats to mix with their old wheat to make it better. We actually allow these people to take the best wheat from us,

No doubt the increase in potatoes was larger on account of the scarcity of potatoes recently. Now take the imports and let us note the difference. They are manufactured articles principally. speechtext:
Somebody possibly may have been asleep at the switch, but I am prepared, and have so stated, to advocate the imposition of a duty so that no eggs whatever will come into this country. 
I will not make it easier for Australian eggs or Chinese eggs or any old eggs to come into Canada either.
Some hon. members have told us in the last few days that the United States are getting tired of the tariff, that they are going to make a change in that respect, that they are going to set matters right, that the people over there are getting sore on the tariff game. We were told that six or seven years ago. If my hon. friends opposite would get some of the old speeches and read them over they will find that the same prediction was made at that time. Do my hon. friends know what happens over there? Each time the product of another country finds its way into the United States they raise the duty a little more. W hat has happened quite recently? The duty on butter put up, the duty on wheat put up, and do you know what will happen next? Have hon. gentlemen observed what occurred the other day? and it is the first premonition of what is going to happen to milk and cream. We have a nice market there at present; we send them eight or ten million dollars' worth. But the other day the report was published all over the country on the authority of the Health Commissioners of New York city that the quality of the milk and cream coming into the United States from Ontario was awful-in fact this gentleman described it as "bootleg" cream, whatever that meant. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture could tell us what bootleg cream is. I do not know what it is myself; perhaps some farmer has been transporting it in his boot. At all events these people are looking for an excuse to exclude our cream. That is all they are doing, and that is just what is going to happen. We were told too by a man who knew that cows were decreasing in the United States. "Why," he said, "the number of cows is going down all the time and the United States are bound to have imports of dairy products soon." But what is happening? I have on my desk the official statistics for the year ending 31st December last. What do we find? The United States imported $10,000,000 of milk and cream practically all from us. Of butter they imported $2,600,000; that is all the butter they imported. They exported butter to the value of $2,400,000. But mark this; in addition to this exportation of butter they exported
151.000.	000 pounds of condensed and powdered milk and cream, to the value of $17,000,000. That country was able to export last year
151.000.	000 pounds of powdered cream, importing only $2,100,000 wo'rth; they exported almost the same quantity of butter, yet they tell us they are going out of the dairy busi-

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin (Lincoln)
ness. If they go out of the business they will have to go into it faster than they are doing in Alberta if they ever hope to catch up.
Another matter of interest to the people of the country is the income tax. I am not opposed to the minister proposing to collect -income taxes from people who are striving to evade taxation by forming joint stock companies, privately held joint stock companies, for the purpose of holding the funds and thus evading taxation. I am absolutely in favour of that proposition of the minister and have no hesitation in saying so. But, Mr. Speaker, under the present proposal there will be injustice. I have in my mind the case of a public utility in my own district which operates electric light, electric power and street railway, which established small concerns in different towns under special charter, and then amalgamated them all under one charter in accordance with the law. Under this law it would seem that these different companies are to be taxed, each one on its profits, and then later the parent company will be taxed also. I do not agree at all with the principle of taxing profits twice, but in this case the profits are not only being taxed twice, but three times, and perhaps in some oases four times. I do not know whether the minister intends to make any change in that regard, but I certainly recommend that he look a little closer into it. I know of many cases of small factories that are held by companies which are entirely within families, and it appears to me that in cases of that kind it is absurd to tax the profits in the concern twice. It is ridiculous to tax the profits of the company and then tax the company again in dividends. It simply cannot be done. It would mean that you would put a premium on people evading the tax, and they can evade it. In those cases it would not be hard for the people themselves who are running the concerns which are privately held to take every dollar by way of salary, and the government would not get a dollar of company income tax at all. Why should you put any of your citizens in that position? It is not fair or right that taxes should be collected from the same money twice. This government has by its actions driven artisans out of this country, and now it proposes to follow that up by driving out the money too. As soon as you begin to tax the dollar beyond what you should, you are going to lose the dollar; just make up your mind to that.
As a matter of record, and not for anything .more than the record, I find that during last 14011-210
year 3,061 farmers paid income tax, and paid in amounts $162,000 out of $56,000,000. Under the new tax levy many thousands of workers escape taxation, but widows and others, dependent upon their income from investments and savings, are taxed heavier than they were before. I think that is wrong and that those resolutions might very properly be amended.
What did the minister say when he spoke of these tax reductions? He said he was pleased to say that he was going to make tax reductions all along the line. Here is what he is reported as saying in Hansard:
With a desire to make available new money for development our proposals provide reductions all along the line.
Is that statement correct? Is it in accordance with the facts? Is the reduction all along the line? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that * there is a decided increase on a great deal of the line, a very decided increase, and that in no case is there any decrease all along the line. As I said before, the taxing of the same profit twice is unfair, and I feel certain that in the end it will not be in the interest of the country or of the treasury itself. I warn the minister that when the dollar is taxed excessively it will get away from us.
I wish to give some examples of the actual working out of some of these proposals, just to show what the result will be. For instance, a married man without dependent children with a salary of $5,000 and a dividend income of $5,000 more, in 1924 paid in taxes $241.50; and now he pays $290. That is no decrease along the line. The married man whose income comes from dividends in Canadian corporations, which have already paid an income tax, and' whose wife has a separate income, on a $10,000 salary in 1924, paid $115.50 income tax. This year under this law he would pay $425, an increase from $115 to $425. On a $20,000 income his tax will be increased from $745 to $1,815, and on a $30,000 income the increase will be from $1,900 to $3,900-not very much decrease along the line there.

An unmarried man with an income of $10,000 derived from dividends in Canadian companies paid last year $115.50; to-day he will pay $415. An unmarried man whose -whole income is from dividends of foreign companies on an income of $10,000 lart year paid $630 whereas

I want to point out some glaring cases. For instances a man who to-day is paying income tax under the clause in regard to incomes from dividend, on a $5,000 income pays 186 per cent more than he paid before. On a $10,000 income the percentage is decreased somewhat; he pays 90 per cent more than he did before. On a $40,000 income the percentage is decreased still further; he pays only 20 per cent more than he paid before.

On a $50,000 income he does not pay any more than he paid before. In other words this proposition is made for the rich man, not for the taxpayer of moderate means. When you come to incomes of more than $50,000 the situation is reversed. This is not a decrease all along the line; it is worse than that. It is an increase part of the line and a decrease on the very end of the line on incomes that can well afford to pay th<~

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin (Lincoln)
tax. When you come to incomes of $60,000 there is a decrease of 5 per cent; when you reach incomes of $70,000 there is a decrease of 13 per cent, and when you reach incomes of $90,000, the decrease is 25 per cent, whereas on the smaller incomes the amount of the tax is increased.
I want to say a word or two now about the Canadian National Railways. Nobody is better pleased than myself, no party is better pleased than we are, in being able to learn from the minister that the fortunes of the National Railways have shown an improvement. I trust the improvement will continue. On looking over the financial statement of the Canadian National Railways I find very little information as to expenditures on capital or branch lines and even less information as to the question of hotels. It seems to me that the shareholders of this corporation have the right to receive information on these particular items. I have lately seen it frequently stated in the press that it is in the mind of someone to enlarge the Chateau Laurier. Surely the minister does not propose any such thing as this; surely we have enough capital expenditure now. If the minister could demonstrate that these hotels had made money, the matter would be different, but I understand that every one of them has been showing losses for years. In that case why on earth we should embark on more expenditures for hotels is beyond my comprehension.
I wish to refer to one phase of this financial statement of the National Railways, because it is quite interesting to me and no doubt it will be interesting to some hon. members who have been telling us with so much elation that the profits of the road have been due to the increase in the haulage of grain, and that when you have a good crop year you have a good profit year. That is the argument they used to refute the statement that came from the railway companies directly that they were losing money on the haulage of grain. I find on looking over the tonnage revenue published in the Financial statement of the National Railways, page 33, that of material such as wheat, oats, com, barley, flour and all these things that apply to the farm 144,000 tons less were hauled in 1925 than in 1924. If anybody can show me how you can produce an increase in profits by hauling less stuff I will give him the palm unless it be that when you are losing money on hauling material, the less you haul the better off you are. That is just what has happened in this case. For the year there is an earned profit of $32,000,000 over and above the overhead of the railway and not 14011-2l0i
one cent of that was earned on the grain. That is evident on the face of the report, and if anybody were to deny it I would feel like applying to have his head read.
Where does the profit come from? The second lot of products that were hauled were products of animals and the quantity was reduced by 12,000 tons, so that no profit can be figured from that. The products of the mines show an increase in haulage of 671,000 tons. The produets of the forest eaime up with another addition of 360,000 tons, while in the products of manufactures and miscellaneous commodities there was an increase of 1,626 000 tons. And these three articles provided the $15,000,000 profit, less of course what was made by savings. Undoubtedly the statement show, and shows quite clearly, that savings were made in expenses. The report indicates emphatically-it is as plain as the nose on a man's face-that not one cent of that profit came from the things which hon. gentlemen of the Progressive party suggest. Not a dollar of the new money came from that source at all.

If it happened this year then there was not as much grain moved as there was last year. In this business as in any other you have to spread your expenses over the year. This applies in railroading just as it does in manufacturing, and probably more so. Certain expenses in connection with the purchase of this, that and the other necessity must be spread over the year, and the account is not made up until the latter end of the year. That is what might happen in this particular case.
I want to impress upon the House the fact that while the Canadian National Railways have had a year of improved business they have still some distance to go before they are out of the woods, so to speak. According to the statement of the Canadian National Railways the deficit increased by $41,000,000. Now, we can congratulate ourselves upon the assumption that the road has pretty nearly paid its way, but you have to remember that the government is not getting one cent of interest for the large amount of money which it has invested in the railways. Indeed, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Roob) says, that investment may have to be written down. Be that as it may, the fact is that we did not earn enough to pay even the whole of the interest that was due the outside bondholders; we were eight or ten million dollars short in that direction. There is, therefore, no use in our shaking hands with ourselves before we have passed the other stile. We have a long way yet to go, and there is no reason why we should talk about reducing rates. I want to stay the minister's hand' from reducing rates to some of our friends for fear they may postpone the day when the railways will get upon a parity basis. The government of Canada have had to step into the breach and pay eight or ten million dollars to meet the interest upon bonds that were held by outsiders, and it has taken no money on account of its own investment in the road. True enough, the situation is improved, and I am glad of it. But the Canadian people do not want to lose sight of the main fact of the case, and the actual situation is as I have stated.
Last year the Minister of Finance, when he had to perform the duty of announcing a decrease in revenue of something like $50,000,000, made a virtue of necessity and took credit for having reduced taxation to that extent. He said, "we have been fifteen or twenty millions short in our sales tax collections and fifteen or twenty millions short in 
the customs tax. Consequently we have relieved you of so much taxation." I assume that, having treated that decline in revenue of $50,000,000 odd as so much of a reduction in taxation, the minister this year, with an increase in revenue of some $30,000,000, will put the shoe on the other foot and admit an increase of taxes on the people to that extent. That, I think, is a reasonable proposition: surely the argument cuts both ways. I notice that last year when it came to customs taxation my hon. friends to the left were quite pleased to see the amount reduced. I want to ask them how they feel now that customs taxation has increased from $108,000,000 to $127,000,000. Is the difference a matter of taxation this year, or is it an increase in revenue? Last year when there was a reduction the minister declared that he had relieved the people to that extent: now that he has increased his collections what does he say? The Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), smiles. Probably he will tell us what the Minister of Finance thinks.

This is the largest item next to customs revenue, and yet we are told that taxation is being reduced.
It was this government who increased the sales tax, and it is not now proposed to lessen that burden at all. The people are told that they will not be allowed to lick the stamps for the receipt tax; that the postage has been reduced, and some other. little things done, which are not noticeable at all. The big taxes remain, however, and the big expenditures also remain. The trouble with this government

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin (Lincoln)
is that they do not know enough to economize. The hon. member who preceded me delivered a long lecture on economy; it was too 'bad the minister did not hear it because the hon. member who is just from the provincial House told us all about taxation, and how economical the provincial government was. This government is spending too much money; taxes are too high; we are not going to be able to compete with our great neighbour to the south unless taxation is reduced. This reduction announced by the minister is no reduction at all, but is simply an adjustment of taxes. Taxes are imposed upon those least able to bear them, and taxes are removed from those who can pay. That is what has been done with the income tax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when the House rose at six o'clock I was discussing the question of taxes and expenditure. Now I want to refer for a moment or two to the public debt. The public debt for the period from 1920 to 1926 inclusive stood each year as follows, in round figures:
1920		 $2,248,000,000
1921		 2,340,000,000
1922		 2,422,000,000
1923		 2,453,000,000
1924		 2,417,000,000
1925		 2,417,000,000
1926		 2,395,000,000
It will be noticed that even with the credits of the present year the debt stands at $55,000,000 more than it did in 1921. There is this further fact which I consider of prime importance: In an ordinary business when a debt is paid that was incurred in or returned from a former year, we usually credit that to suspense account; we do not treat it as a part of that particular year's business. It would be misleading and wrong to say that that was the profit on that particular year's business. My contention is that any money of that sort that came in during the last fiscal year should by right be passed at once to the public debt account and should have gone for the reduction of the public debt. Had the sum we received from Great Britain on various accounts also been credited to the public debt, there would have been a greater reduction of that debt by eighty or ninety million than there is to-day. But the present government placed those receipts into the regular account just as they did in the case of other regular governmental receipts. They treated it as an item of that character and did not apply it as they should have done to the reduction of the public debt.
We have heard nothing from the Minister of Finance in respect to the Roumanian and
3306	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Chaplin (Lincoln)
Grecian loans. We have not been told whether these countries have paid their obligations to Canada. Last year the government took the credit for the payment before it was known whether Roumania or Greece were going to pay or not. They have not told us anything this year as to whether these countries have kept up their payments or not; we know nothing about it.
Now I come to a consideration of the tariff resolutions announced from the budget. The first item has to do with some of the treaties that have been entered into. We had to change our tariff in conformity with some of the treaties that were made a short time ago. The first item on the schedule is meats. In other words the members in this House who are free traders, who will not stand for any kind of protection, are quite satisfied to raise the duty on meats for the benefit of another *country. Why was the duty on meats raised in this case? For the benefit of Canada? Oh, no, for the benefit of Australia! Some hon. gentlemen are free traders but they can stand being protectionists for Australia. I would ask these hon. gentlemen if they will not be protectionists for the sake of their own country? Protection is good enough when it applies to some other country, but it is of no use in the interests of Canada. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), need not laugh. Hon. gentlemen opposite go to the West Indies and make a treaty, and then they come back and submit to this House increased duties on lines of goods that are intended for the protection of people of these islands and not for the protection of the people of Canada. For example there is cocoa, coffee, ginger, nutmegs and arrowroot. If the ministry would pay a little more attention to their own people rather than to the people of other countries they would accomplish more good.
In the tariff resolutions there is a long schedule with respect to sugar. This government have changed the sugar schedule three times for the protection of the coloured people in the West Indies and to the detriment of the people of this Dominion, particularly to the disadvantage of three or four counties in the province of Ontario. This government do not believe in protection for the farmers of the counties of Kent, Lambton and Essex, but they do believe in that policy when it comes to helping coloured labour in the West Indies. That is the kind of protection that hon. gentlemen from Saskatchewan and other provinces of the west are voting for.
(Mr. J. D. Chaplin.]
There is an item in the schedule dealing with the duty on table salt. The Minister of Finance offered no explanation when he announced the item, but here it is. The article is not pure salt. It contains some mixture permitting it to enter on a basis of five per cent, ten per cent and fifteen per cent respectively. It may be all right, but it does not seem to me that it is going to be of any particular benefit to the salt industry of this country. I find also such things as bananas and fruits of all kinds, fruits that are not produced in this country at all, but as to which we are quite satisfied to tax ourselves in the interests of the people of some other country. That may be good business for those people but it does not appear to be very good business for us. I would rather put taxes upon something that would protect the Canadian people instead of the people of some other country.
Passing from the sugar schedule, the next item is "angostura bitters". I think some comment has been made upon this item already. This is where the cocktail comes into use. In the interests of those gentlemen who want to use angostura bitters the duty is reduced from $10 to $5. Can it be argued that such a reduction as that is for the benefit of the workingmen and the farmers of this country?
We come now to the serious item, which has caused a good deal of talk throughout the country, namely, the automobile schedule. Before discussing that schedule I should like, for the information of the House, to disclose what takes place in the department. We have a Finance department which makes the laws respecting duties, and then we have a Customs department which is the executive and carries out the laws that are laid down by the Finance department. When the duties were placed upon automobiles they were fixed at 35 per cent. At the time those duties were imposed no provision whatever was made in respect of the parts. Parts were not mentioned at all, and consequently the Customs department had to make a regulation covering what were parts of automobiles. In their judgment, and with the knowledge they had, they decided that the parts of an automobile consisted of the following; the wheels, the chassis, the top and the body. That constituted an automobile, and those were all the parts of an automobile. Of course the inconsistency of any such ruling will be quite apparent to anybody when I tell you that the parts of a wheel would not be considered as parts of an automobile. For instance, while a wheel is a part of the car, the hub of a wheel would not be part of a

The Budget-Mr'. Chaplin (Lincoln)
car. That is the style of business that is being carried on in the Customs department.
I am not blaming this government or any one at all, but I simply say those are matters which grew up in the department. The people in the department are not acquainted with the business they are handling.
The other day, in order to obtain some information from the department, I visited the place to ascertain the conditions there.
I asked one of the chief clerks what the duty on an automobile hub was, and what do you suppose he told me? He looked through the list and found "hub blocks", and he said "the duty on that would be the same as on "hub blocks". Those who have been here for a number of years know very well that the hub block was a block made for the old style of carriage. It was an dm Mock with a hole through it, and this officer was going to fix the duty on automobile hubs the same as the duty on a hub block used twenty years ago! That is an illustration of the knowledge some people have of the business. When I tell the House that in an automobile there are 160 or 200 parts which have to be made or brought in-at any rate they have to be provided-for the manufacture of a car, you can see how far you can get with a department which decides in its own judgment that there are only four parts to an automobile. You can see the inconsistency and the foolishness of trying to work a Finance department and have the Customs department interpret what is in the minister's mind. I am not criticizing the minister for that at all. My remarks are not based upon that suggestion. I hope that possibly some good may come from my remarks and that it may be so arranged that men in the Finance department will know what they are doing, and what they want, or that the other people will find out what they want and do it. But that is certainly not the case in this instance.
Now we come to this situation. We find the minister has put in the tariff schedule a clause that now covers, as far as I can make out, parts of automobiles, but parts of automobiles evidently are not going to be the same parts as they were before. They mujt change that. What is going to be done is hard to say. One thing is sure, namely, that this clause and this automobile business cannot be properly, definitely and reasonably discussed before we see what changes are going to be made. There must be some changes. I warn the minister that under the present proposed tariff this business runs a chance of being ruined, I do not care what anybody says. Unless some changes are made
the business is gone. The parts man cannot stay in business unless the automobile man remains in business. It is impossible, because if a car comes in and certain parts are to be made here, it does not make any difference how cheaply they can be manufactured here, they will never get on that car. The same thing applies to tires. If automobiles complete are allowed to come in at low rates of duty, the tire man may be willing to make his tires as cheaply as possible, yet there is no chance on earth of his getting the business; consequently you run the risk of putting the parts man out of business unless you conserve the automobile business. If, on the other hand, you decide that the automobile people can function by bringing in the car mostly manufactured, or over half manufactured, you still put your parts men on the block and their investment in this country is gone.
The hon. minister said the other day, " I discussed this matter with automobile people." He did not say that in the House, but he made that statement; I do not suppose it was particularly private. But as far as I know he never discussed the matter with the parts people and they never had a chance to discuss it with him before they came down. Here is an industry about which the minister had not the proper information. He could not get it from the Customs department, because they did not know anything about it and do not yet. He gets information from one or two sources, and I will warrant you that the information the minister got since he made the changes is a lot more than he got previously; he knows more about the difficulties now than he ever knew before. It would have been a good deal better if he had got the information a little ahead of time.
But somebody says that the people knew these changes were going to be made. The truth of the matter is that the automobile people relied on the statement of the Prime Minister, made in the cities which he visited; they relied upon his statement that there would be no changes in the tariff and that he was appointing a tariff commission. The people expected to make their representations to the proper place, and the tariff board was the place for them to go. I am not saying whether the tariff is too high or too low; I do not care, but I say that no government has any right to strike at the heart of any industry without making a proper and careful analysis of the whole situation. That in my opinion has not been done. The argument is used that Mr. Henry Ford says that automobiles are too dear. He wants free trade

I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not in the chamber because I want to refer to one more item on the schedule. Hon. members will remember that some years ago I stated in this House that I approached the late Minister of Finance, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, with the request that' he place a duty on the dyeing of silk. There was no duty in 1921 upon the article that it was proposed to put on the market and the manufacturer who was desirous of coming here to do the dyeing asked for 10 per cent protection. The minister said: Of course we are not a protectionist government and I will not make
any promises, but if it looks reasonable to us I will consider the matter. In the 1922 budget the minister was good enough to place a duty of 10 per cent upon the silk dyeing industry and in my locality about $100,000 were spent by a small firm in establishing a silk dyeing industry. It so happened that the minister, along with the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who afterwards became Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), went over to France and made a treaty with that country. By means of that treaty about one-half of the duty was cut off.
I want to refer to another act of perfidy, or, Mr. Speaker, if you consider that too strong a word, let me say another breach of faith on the part of this government. A couple of years ago, I believe in 1924, an English concern came to Canada and approached this government with a view to having a duty imposed on artificial silk, which product they were prepared to make. This company, I may say, is the largest English concern in the silk industry and one of the foremost companies of the kind in the world. They came here and interviewed the minister, submitting certain proposals as to what they would do. They offered to erect a plant at a cost of between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000 and to utilize our wood product in the making of artificial silk. We do not know what took place but at any rate the government met them, and following that interview a duty was imposed on this article At the same time a drawback was provided for the purpose of allowing people interested in the importation of this commodity to bring in their supplies in the meantime until the factory should be started. Mr. Fielding in 1923 at page 2648 of Hansard volume 3 is reported as follows:
A ncsw industry is promised us for tihe manufacture o-f artificial silk. It is represented to us that this industry will employ a large amount of labour and we have every reason to believe that if we can make encouraging terms a great industry will be established. We propose to make a classification in which it will be treated largely as silk, and we have every reason to hope this will lead to a very' important industry being established.
The Englishmen, it appears, were not quite satisfied with the lengths to which the minister had gone, and after some further negotiations the resolutions were changed in committee to meet their views, with the result that they got the terms they desired. The drawbacks were also arranged. The company afterwards wrote to the minister and told him that they were going to be somewhat late in getting their mill going. They wanted to make sure first that their product was a success, and so
